'''''Artemisia arborescens''''', the '''tree wormwood''', is a [[species]] of flowering plant in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Asteraceae]], [[native plant|native]] to the [[Mediterranean]] region.<ref>[https://luirig.altervista.org/flora/taxa/index1.php?scientific-name=artemisia+arborescens Altervista Flora Italiana, Assenzio arbustivo ''Artemisia arborescens'' (Vaill.) L.]</ref> It is an erect [[evergreen]] [[perennial plant|perennial]], with masses of finely-divided aromatic silvery-white leaves and single-sided sprays of yellow daisy-like flowers. This plant is cultivated for its foliage effects, but in colder [[temperateness|temperate]] regions it requires the protection of a wall.

The [[Botanical name#Binary name|specific epithet]] ''arborescens'' means "woody" or "tree-like".<ref name=RHSLG>{{cite book|last=Harrison|first=Lorraine|title=RHS Latin for gardeners|year=2012|publisher=Mitchell Beazley|location=United Kingdom|isbn=9781845337315|pages=224}}</ref>

This plant<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Artemisia arborescens''|url=
https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/1627/Artemisia-arborescens/Details | accessdate=23 February 2020}}</ref> and the [[cultivar]] 'Powis Castle'<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Artemisia arborescens'' 'Powis Castle'|url=
https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/92327/Artemisia-Powis-Castle/Details|accessdate=14 April 2020}}</ref> have gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite book|title=RHS A-Z encyclopedia of garden plants|year=2008|publisher=Dorling Kindersley|location=United Kingdom|isbn=978-1405332965|pages=1136}}</ref>

'Powis Castle' is relatively compact, and unlike typical ''A. arborescens'', it rarely flowers. It has a strong sweet smell, quite different from that of ''A. arborescens''. It has been suggested to be a hybrid between ''A. arborescens'' and ''A. absinthium'', but is probably a form from the Middle East where ''arborescems'' and ''absinthium'' appear to intergrade. The original source is unknown, but British gardener Jim Hancock took a cutting of a plant that he found growing during a garden visit in Yorkshire {{Circa|1968}}, and took it to [[Powis Castle]] when he became Head Gardener there in 1972. It was later named from that garden, propagated and sold to promote the [[National Trust]] gardens.<ref>JD Twibell, Plant Identification from Vapour Analysis, The Plantsman 14 (3) 184-190 1992</ref>

This plant, like others of the [[genus]] ''[[Artemisia (genus)|Artemisia]]'', yields [[essential oil]]s which have historically been used for various medicinal purposes, and its pharmacological properties are under investigation.<ref>{{Cite journal|doi = 10.1186/1476-0711-6-10|title = Antiherpevirus activity of Artemisia arborescens essential oil and inhibition of lateral diffusion in Vero cells|year = 2007|last1 = Saddi|first1 = Manuela|last2 = Sanna|first2 = Adriana|last3 = Cottiglia|first3 = Filippo|last4 = Chisu|first4 = Lorenza|last5 = Casu|first5 = Laura|last6 = Bonsignore|first6 = Leonardo|last7 = De Logu|first7 = Alessandro|journal = Annals of Clinical Microbiology and Antimicrobials|volume = 6|page = 10|pmid = 17894898|pmc = 2099429 | doi-access=free }}</ref> It also has culinary uses, including as a substitute for or supplement to [[spearmint]] in [[Maghrebi mint tea]] during the winter (when mint is out of season), imparting a bitter flavor.<ref name=Artemisia_guide>{{citation |date=2013 |title=Artemisia: An Essential Guide from The Herb Society of America |publisher=The Herb Society of America |url=http://www.herbsociety.org/herbs/documents/artemisia_guide_final-1_000.pdf |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20150905120137/http://www.herbsociety.org/herbs/documents/artemisia_guide_final-1_000.pdf |archivedate=2015-09-05 }}</ref>
